hardware.name: NVIDIA DGX Spark
hardware.note: torch.cuda.get_arch_list() on this part returns sm_80/90/100/110/120 -- nothing is built for 12.1. That gap is the point of this arena.

upstream.note: upstream ggml-org master; the fork carries 5 commits on top of it (laguna arch port + DFlash draft). The arch port is upstreamed as ggml-org/llama.cpp#25595, unmerged at pin time. 'What changed vs stock' = these 5 commits plus your diff.

editablePathsNote: CUDA kernels and the model graph. Deliberately NOT editable: tools/server (the thing being measured), common/, tests/, and the CMake build definition -- a submission that changes how it is timed is not a submission.

gates.rule: git diff vendor base->candidate touches only editablePaths, and the target's model integrity (file sha256 + param count from /props) is unchanged.
For every public prompt: candidate output is byte-identical to the target's golden, at batch 1, greedy, warmup discarded.
Same, on prompts the submitter has never seen. Run by the referee only.
gates.mechanism: Prompts are GENERATED from a random seed at verification time, never stored. A file in a public repo is visible; a gitignored file on the referee's node is a static set that leaks a little with every verification. Generating instead means nobody -- including the referee -- knows the prompts in advance, and the seed is recorded in the result so anyone can regenerate them afterwards to audit a disputed verification. Unknowable ahead, reproducible behind.
gates.goldens: None are stored. The base arm computes them in the same session, back to back with the candidate -- which is also what makes them impossible to tune against.
gates.promotionRequires: A passing record file, not a flag. `promote --held-out-record <path>` checks the record targets the same slug AND was produced against the same changed files as the bench record -- verifying one diff and promoting another is the obvious way to launder a failing submission.
gates.catches: A kernel that reassociated its way into a different argmax on everything except the prompts it was tuned against.

gates.rule: decode_speedup >= 0.95 AND prefill_speedup >= 0.95. Hard floors -- you cannot trade prefill away for decode.
score > current leaderboard score for every target claimed.

scoring.pairing: Speedups are paired ratios: baseline and candidate arms run back to back, alternating, in the same session on the same node. The ratio cancels host and thermal drift -- which is not theoretical here (a published baseline failed to reproduce a day later, 24.05 -> 20.09 tok/s).

measurement.warmupNote: The first request after server start differs on BOTH engines. Discard it or every comparison reports a phantom mismatch.

determinism.vllm: 12/12 identical (0.26.0) at batch 1; n=2 -> 2 distinct, n=6 -> 5 distinct
determinism.consequence: Any batching breaks token identity, so the ranked track is serial. This is not a limitation to route around; it is what makes the cheap correctness gate possible at all.

thermalGate.note: mlxfast uses a fixed 40 C. The Spark idles around 43 C and has been observed at 84 C under sustained load while its sibling idled at 43, so 40 is unreachable and copying it would deadlock the gate.

measured.note: Two consecutive baseline arms both ran 46 -> 56 C and both took ~60 s to fall back under the ceiling. A ranked arm heats this part by 10 C, repeatably. 46 costs about a minute of waiting per arm and is what makes the arms comparable; do not raise it to save that minute.

multiNode.note: A target may declare nodeCount > 1. Plenty of Spark owners have two or more, and clustered recipes (TP2 over ConnectX, llama.cpp RPC) are a first-class part of the corpus -- an arena that only ranks single-node work would exclude the recipes that most need kernel help.
requirements: Every node passes the thermal gate before an arm starts, not just the head. One hot worker is enough to make a paired ratio meaningless, and it is the node you are not watching.

The candidate tree is synced to every node before its arm. A worker still running the base build silently measures a mixed cluster -- the worst failure mode here, because it produces a plausible number rather than an error.
Every node is verified idle. On a 2-node run the head is the one you notice; the worker is where somebody else's job hides.
The interconnect is declared and checked (a 200G ConnectX link that negotiated 10/100 has happened on this fleet, and it looks like a kernel regression).
multiNode.blockedOn: Whether greedy token identity survives a collective (NCCL allreduce under TP). Unmeasured. Concurrency already breaks identity at n=2 on one node, so this cannot be assumed -- and it is a property of the collective, not of any one model, so one measurement settles it for every multi-node target.

crossBootIdentity.why: Gates 2 and 3 compare a BASE-tree server against a CANDIDATE-tree server. Those are two processes, so the whole cheap gate rests on greedy output surviving a restart -- not merely on it being stable within one server.
crossBootIdentity.llamaCpp: HOLDS. Two boots an hour apart, separate warmups, 4/4 prompts byte-identical (2026-07-28). This is the load-bearing property of the arena, not a bonus.
crossBootIdentity.vllm: HOLDS under a pinned serve config (2026-07-28, supersedes the 07-27 finding). Three boots of Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4 on 0.26.0 were identical across boots both with --enforce-eager and with cudagraphs on, so capture is not the cause and a deterministic vLLM config does not have to pay eager execution. The pins that matter: --max-num-seqs 1, --kv-cache-memory-bytes, --max-model-len, --gpu-memory-utilization and a shared VLLM_CACHE_ROOT. The earlier five-boot failure used --max-num-seqs 4, which is the prime suspect -- batch shape already flips the argmax on this part at n=2.
crossBootIdentity.consequence: A vLLM arena is possible. The difference from llama.cpp is that vLLM must publish a PINNED SERVE CONFIG as part of the measurement contract, the same way it publishes the prompt set -- llama.cpp is cross-boot identical under an ordinary serve command.

policy.optimizationVsRecipe: Optimizations preserve output and get the cheap gate. Changes that alter output (precision, quantization, sampling) are a new RECIPE, not an arena submission, and need eval evidence on howtospark.com.
policy.scoreScope: A submission names the targets it claims. Engine-general changes score across all targets; model-specific ones score on one. A claim of 'faster Q4_K MoE matmul' where a dense Q8_0 target also moves is incoherent and does not promote.
policy.baselineAfterPromotion: OPEN QUESTION -- mlxfast re-pins the baseline to the frontier. Until decided, the baseline is the vendor pin above and every score is only meaningful against contractVersion 1.
